criteria.quote: Magmar heals wounds by dipping them in lava.
criteria.revision: Open with the sharper contrast: “Magmar heals a wound by dipping it in lava—then, when tired, it leaps into a volcano to soak.”

criteria.quote: Then it soaks its body in magma to ease its weariness.
How does Magmar turn a lava bath into recovery?
criteria.revision: Use the two documented cases to create a clearer open question: “How can lava treat Magmar’s wounds and ease its weariness?”

criteria.quote: Its body burns constantly, and magma eases its weariness.
criteria.revision: Replace the final repetition with a new concrete detail: “Its body burns at 2,192 degrees Fahrenheit—and hotter places make Alolan Magmar feel better.”

criteria.quote: But tired Magmar goes further: it leaps into a volcano.
criteria.revision: Delay this reveal until after the wound treatment, then frame it as the escalation: “A wound is only one reason Magmar enters lava. When tired, it leaps into a volcano and soaks its body in magma.”

criteria.quote: Magmar heals wounds by dipping them in lava. / The Pokédex says Magmar can heal a wound in lava.
criteria.revision: Remove the second scene or replace it with a distinct fact: “Magmar was born in an active volcano, and its body is always cloaked in flames.”

criteria.quote: Magmar's lava bath handles both wounds and weariness, matching the hot-spring comparison in its Pokédex.
criteria.revision: Make the ending synthesize the two uses instead of repeating the premise: “A wound gets dipped into lava; weariness sends Magmar into a full magma soak—the Pokédex really does compare it to a hot spring.”

criteria.quote: Healing method or extreme endurance test?
criteria.revision: Ask a split grounded in the two entries: “Does Magmar’s lava soak work better as a hot-spring comparison for wounds, weariness, or both?”
